zh.q: 一块银白色的小金属，为什么必须泡在煤油里，着火时连水都不能浇？
zh.concl: 钠原子的最外电子层上只有 1 个电子，在化学反应中该电子很容易失去，因此钠的化学性质非常活泼、表现出很强的还原性（教材原话）。本课用四个站位把这一句话变成四件看得见的事。
points: 一块钠要讲四件事：怎么放、怎么烧、遇水怎样、着火怎么办。
每个站位都有一块「没做这个操作」的对照钠，颜色差才看得出来。
不要用手直接接触钠，而要用镊子夹取（教材 p.34 的注意框）。

zh.q: 刚切开的钠亮得发光，为什么十几秒就暗了？
zh.concl: 新切开的钠的光亮的表面很快变暗了，这是因为钠与氧气发生反应，在钠的表面生成了一薄层氧化物，这种氧化物是氧化钠：4Na + O₂ = 2Na₂O（教材原话）。所以钠在空气中变质是氧化还原反应（教材 p.43 练习 4 的答案）。
points: 「变暗」不是脏了，是表面生成了一薄层 Na₂O。
光泽从 100 % 一路掉到 0.2 %，钠一直在失电子：0.0 → 8.7 mmol。
曲线图上实线（敞口）掉得很快、虚线（泡在煤油里）几乎不动。

zh.q: 那怎么才能让它不变暗？
zh.concl: 教材 p.35：要把钠保存在石蜡油或煤油中，以隔绝空气。煤油把空气挡住，钠就接触不到 O₂，也就不会变暗。
points: 挡住的是空气里的 O₂，不是钠本身——「隔绝空气」四个字就是煤油的全部作用。
同样 300 s：敞口 8.7 mmol、煤油 1.9 mmol，差 4.6 倍。
操作上还要「用镊子取一小块钠，用滤纸吸干表面的煤油」（教材【实验2-1】第一步）。

zh.q: 把它加热，钠会变成什么？为什么不是氧化钠？
zh.concl: 钠受热后先熔化，然后与氧气剧烈反应，发出黄色火焰，生成一种淡黄色固体——过氧化钠：2Na + O₂ =△= Na₂O₂（教材原话）。钠燃烧生成的是 Na₂O₂，不是 Na₂O（教材 p.43 练习 3 把「钠燃烧时生成氧化钠」判为错项）。
points: 常温与加热是两种不同产物：Na₂O（灰白）与 Na₂O₂（淡黄）——颜色一变就是证据。
钠先熔化，是因为它的熔点只有 97.79 ℃（教材 p.34 数据卡）。
不要近距离俯视坩埚（教材 p.35 的注意框）。

zh.q: 把钠丢进滴了酚酞的水里，会看到什么？
zh.concl: 钠的性质非常活泼，能与水发生剧烈反应；反应时放出热量；反应后得到的溶液显碱性（教材原话）：2Na + 2H₂O = 2NaOH + H₂↑。红色是生成的 NaOH 遇酚酞变出来的，不是钠本身变红。
points: 五个字各有依据：浮←密度 0.97 < 1.00；熔←放热、超过熔点 97.79 ℃；游·响←生成 H₂ 气体；红←溶液显碱性（教材 p.36 只给「位置 / 形状 / 溶液颜色」三个观察角度，五字是通行归纳）。
对照烧杯没滴酚酞：无色，但 pH 一样是 12.94——碱性是反应给的，酚酞只是显示剂。
不要近距离俯视烧杯（教材 p.36 的注意框）。

zh.q: 换一块大一点的钠，会有什么不同？
zh.concl: 方程式给出了比例：2Na + 2H₂O = 2NaOH + H₂↑——每 2 个钠放 1 个 H₂、生成 2 个 NaOH。钠越多，H₂ 越多、NaOH 越浓、溶液越碱、操作也越危险。
points: 钠块越大，反应越剧烈、放出 H₂ 越多、碱性越强、风险越高——四个读数同向变。
但 1 g 钠的读数是不变的（43.5 mmol 电子、487.0 mL H₂）：变的是量的多少，不是反应本身。
pH 只从 12.64 涨到 13.94，因为 pH 是对数刻度。

zh.q: 钠在这四个站位里做的其实是同一件事？
zh.concl: 教材 p.34：原子的最外电子层上只有 1 个电子，在化学反应中该电子很容易失去。所以钠跟氧气、跟水、跟燃烧时的 O₂ 反应，做的都是同一件事——失去 1 个电子变成 Na⁺。这也是主读数 n(e⁻) 与反应对象无关的原因。
points: 四个站位、四种现象，微观上是同一件事：Na − e⁻ → Na⁺。
所以主读数 n(e⁻) 只随钠的多少变，不随「跟谁反应」变（这一步是它的立身之本）。
Na₂O₂ 里的氧不是 −2 价，所以它既能被氧化又能被还原（教材 p.43 练习 2(3) 要求你从这个角度分析它）。

zh.q: 钠着火了，水不能浇、CO₂ 灭火器也不能用——那该用什么？
zh.concl: 教材 p.37：活泼金属着火时，不能用水灭火，可使用专用灭火剂或干砂灭火。水不能用，是因为钠与水剧烈反应、放热并放出可燃的 H₂（p.37）；CO₂ 灭火器不能用，是因为钠燃烧生成的 Na₂O₂ 与 CO₂ 反应反而放出 O₂：2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ = 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂（p.37）。
points: 错误操作「浇水」→ 风险 0.91、火势加剧：钠遇水放热、放出 H₂，等于往火上加油。
错误操作「CO₂ 灭火器」→ 风险 0.79、火势更旺：Na₂O₂ 与 CO₂ 放出 O₂，CO₂ 反倒成了供氧剂。
正确做法：干沙土覆盖，把空气隔开，风险 0.07、火熄灭；钠块越大风险越高（0.07 → 0.16），但仍在安全档里。

zh.q: 把这场钠火扑灭，并把风险压进安全档
zh.concl: 只有干砂（或专用灭火剂）能灭火：它把空气隔开，既不把水带进反应，也不像 CO₂ 那样给 Na₂O₂ 送氧。钠块越小，火越容易控制。
points: 目标有两半：灭火方式换成干沙土，风险指数压到 ≤ 0.10（等价于钠块 ≤ 0.86 g）。
两种干扰（CO₂、水）都来自第 8 步讲过的错误操作，认得出就能立刻拨回去。
钠块越大，沙土档的风险也越高（0.20 g 时 0.07、1.50 g 时 0.13、2.00 g 时 0.16）——所以「沙土」之外还得把块弄小。

en.q: Why must a small silvery-white piece of metal be kept under kerosene, and why can't you even pour water on it when it catches fire?
en.concl: The outer electron shell of a sodium atom has only 1 electron, which is easily lost in chemical reactions, so sodium is chemically very active and a strong reducing agent (textbook wording). This lesson turns that one sentence into four visible things at four stations.
points: One piece of sodium, four things to cover: how to store it, how it burns, what water does, what to do when it catches fire.
Each station has a control piece of sodium that didn't get the treatment, so the color difference is visible.
Never touch sodium with your hands; pick it up with tweezers (warning box, textbook p.34).

en.q: Freshly cut sodium is dazzlingly shiny, so why does it dull within seconds?
en.concl: The shiny surface of freshly cut sodium soon dulls because sodium reacts with oxygen and forms a thin layer of oxide on its surface; this oxide is sodium oxide: 4Na + O₂ = 2Na₂O (textbook wording). So sodium spoiling in air is a redox reaction (answer to textbook p.43 Exercise 4).
points: "Dulling" isn't dirt; it's a thin layer of Na₂O forming on the surface.
Luster falls from 100 % to 0.2 % while sodium keeps losing electrons: 0.0 → 8.7 mmol.
On the chart the solid line (open to air) drops fast while the dashed line (under kerosene) hardly moves.

en.q: So how do you stop it dulling?
en.concl: Textbook p.35: sodium is stored in paraffin oil or kerosene to keep air out. Kerosene blocks the air, so sodium can't reach O₂ and won't dull.
points: What is blocked is the O₂ in air, not the sodium itself; "keeping air out" is the whole job of kerosene.
Same 300 s: open 8.7 mmol, kerosene 1.9 mmol, a 4.6× difference.
In practice you also "take a small piece of sodium with tweezers and blot the kerosene off its surface with filter paper" (first step of textbook Experiment 2-1).

en.q: What does sodium turn into when heated, and why isn't it sodium oxide?
en.concl: When heated, sodium first melts, then reacts violently with oxygen, giving a yellow flame and a pale-yellow solid, sodium peroxide: 2Na + O₂ =△= Na₂O₂ (textbook wording). Burning sodium forms Na₂O₂, not Na₂O (textbook p.43 Exercise 3 marks "burning sodium forms sodium oxide" as the wrong option).
points: Room temperature and heating give two different products: Na₂O (grayish white) and Na₂O₂ (pale yellow); the color change is the evidence.
Sodium melts first because its melting point is only 97.79 ℃ (textbook p.34 data card).
Don't look down into the crucible from close up (warning box, textbook p.35).

en.q: Drop sodium into water with phenolphthalein: what do you see?
en.concl: Sodium is very active and reacts violently with water; the reaction releases heat and the resulting solution is basic (textbook wording): 2Na + 2H₂O = 2NaOH + H₂↑. The red comes from the NaOH produced meeting phenolphthalein, not from sodium itself.
points: Each word has a reason: floats ← density 0.97 < 1.00; melts ← heat released, above the 97.79 ℃ melting point; darts · hisses ← H₂ gas produced; red ← the solution is basic (textbook p.36 only gives three angles: position / shape / solution color; the five words are a common teaching summary).
The control beaker has no phenolphthalein: colorless, but pH still 12.94; the basicity comes from the reaction, phenolphthalein only shows it.
Don't look down into the beaker from close up (warning box, textbook p.36).

en.q: What changes with a larger piece of sodium?
en.concl: The equation fixes the ratio: 2Na + 2H₂O = 2NaOH + H₂↑, every 2 sodium give 1 H₂ and 2 NaOH. More sodium means more H₂, more concentrated NaOH, a more basic solution and a more dangerous operation.
points: The bigger the piece, the more violent the reaction, the more H₂, the stronger the basicity and the higher the risk; all four readings move the same way.
But the readings per 1 g of sodium are fixed (43.5 mmol electrons, 487.0 mL H₂): what changes is the amount, not the reaction itself.
pH only rises from 12.64 to 13.94 because pH is a logarithmic scale.

en.q: Is sodium actually doing the same thing at all four stations?
en.concl: Textbook p.34: the atom's outer shell has only 1 electron, which is easily lost in chemical reactions. So whether sodium reacts with oxygen, with water or with O₂ while burning, it does the same thing: loses 1 electron to become Na⁺. That is also why the main reading n(e⁻) doesn't depend on what it reacts with.
points: Four stations, four observations, one thing at the microscopic level: Na − e⁻ → Na⁺.
So the main reading n(e⁻) changes only with the amount of sodium, not with what it reacts with (this step is the reason for that reading).
The oxygen in Na₂O₂ is not −2, so it can be both oxidized and reduced (textbook p.43 Exercise 2(3) asks you to analyze it from this angle).

en.q: Sodium is on fire and you can't use water or a CO₂ extinguisher, so what should you use?
en.concl: Textbook p.37: when an active metal catches fire, don't use water; use a special extinguishing agent or dry sand. Water is ruled out because sodium reacts violently with it, releasing heat and flammable H₂ (p.37); a CO₂ extinguisher is ruled out because the Na₂O₂ formed by burning sodium reacts with CO₂ and actually releases O₂: 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ = 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂ (p.37).
points: Wrong action "pour water" → risk 0.91, fire intensifies: sodium plus water releases heat and H₂, adding fuel to the fire.
Wrong action "CO₂ extinguisher" → risk 0.79, fire burns more fiercely: Na₂O₂ and CO₂ release O₂, so CO₂ ends up supplying oxygen.
Correct action: cover with dry sand to cut off the air, risk 0.07, fire out; larger pieces carry higher risk (0.07 → 0.16) but stay in the safe range.

en.q: Put out this sodium fire and bring the risk into the safe range
en.concl: Only dry sand (or a special agent) works: it cuts off the air, neither bringing water into the reaction nor feeding oxygen to Na₂O₂ the way CO₂ does. The smaller the piece, the easier the fire is to control.
points: The goal has two halves: switch the method to dry sand and bring the risk index to ≤ 0.10 (equivalent to sodium ≤ 0.86 g).
Both disruptions (CO₂, water) are the wrong actions covered in step 8; recognize them and you can switch back at once.
The bigger the piece, the higher the risk even with sand (0.07 at 0.20 g, 0.13 at 1.50 g, 0.16 at 2.00 g), so besides sand you also have to make the piece smaller.
